topic: WHO 2019 criteria: sessile serrated lesion vs hyperplastic polyp
heading: WHO 2019 criteria: sessile serrated lesion vs hyperplastic polyp
text: The WHO 2019 (5th edition) criterion is deliberately low-threshold: a single unequivocal architecturally distorted serrated crypt is sufficient to diagnose a sessile serrated lesion (SSL), whereas a hyperplastic polyp (HP) by definition shows no such distortion. This replaced the WHO 2010 (4th edition) requirement for two or three contiguous characteristic crypts.

question: Q1
topic: WHO 2019 criteria: sessile serrated lesion vs hyperplastic polyp
heading: Terminology and framework
text: The 5th edition formally adopted "sessile serrated lesion" (SSL), retiring sessile serrated adenoma (SSA), sessile serrated polyp (SSP), and SSA/P. [1][5][6] Serrated polyps are classified as hyperplastic polyp, sessile serrated lesion (± dysplasia), and traditional serrated adenoma, with a residual category "serrated adenoma, unclassified." The clinical stakes are substantial: SSLs are precursors to roughly 15-30% of colorectal cancers via the BRAF-mutated, CpG island methylator (CIMP-high) serrated pathway, while HPs carry minimal malignant potential. [1][2][8]

question: Q1
topic: WHO 2019 criteria: sessile serrated lesion vs hyperplastic polyp
heading: The defining architectural criterion for SSL
text:
The hallmark distinguishing SSL from HP is architectural distortion of the crypts, attributed to altered proliferative-zone dynamics. [1] Under the WHO 2019 criteria, the diagnosis requires any of the following features: [1][2][8][9]
- Horizontal growth above the muscularis mucosae — crypts bending to run parallel to the muscularis mucosae, producing L-shaped, boot-shaped, inverted-T, or anchor-shaped silhouettes. [2]
- Dilation of the crypt base — widening of the basal (lower) third of the crypt. [2][8]
- Serrations extending into the crypt base — in contrast to HP, where serration is confined to the upper crypt. [2][8][10]
- Asymmetrical proliferation — the proliferative zone displaced to one side of the crypt with disordered maturation. [2][8]
Critically, the WHO specifies the distortion must be "unequivocal"; subtle architectural change is not sufficient for the diagnosis in the 5th edition, although they commonly co-occur with other abnormalities. [1] Polyp size and location are not part of the histologic criteria, even though SSLs are typically larger and right-sided. [2]
Supportive but non-diagnostic features include mature/dystrophic goblet cells and serration reaching the crypt base ("inverted maturation" or "dysmaturation"), mucosal prolapse/herniation (rare in HP), perineural-like stromal proliferations (>6% of SSLs), and gastric-type mucins (MUC5AC, MUC6). [1][3][11]

topic: WHO 2019 criteria: sessile serrated lesion vs hyperplastic polyp
heading: Hyperplastic polyp criteria (the contrast)
text:
An HP is a serrated polyp with normal crypt architecture and proliferative characteristics. [13] The crypts are elongated but retain a straight, narrow base housing the proliferative zone, with serration confined to the upper half/third of the crypt and no basal dilation, horizontal growth, or L/T-shaped distortion; cytologic dysplasia is absent. [10][12] The WHO recognizes two main subtypes that need not be separated in routine reports: [10][14]
| Feature | Microvesicular HP (MVHP) | Goblet cell-rich HP (GCHP) | References |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Predominant cell mucin | Columnar cells with microvesicular mucin | Mature goblet cells | [10], [14] |
| Serration openings | More prominent, stellate crypt openings | Subtle, surface-limited | [10] |
| BRAF V600E | ~53-76% | ~0-23% | [11], [15] |
| KRAS | ~13-16% | ~46-54% | [15], [16] |
| Likely relationship | Precursor along MVHP $\rightarrow$ SSL continuum | Possible TSA precursor | [3], [11], [17] |

question: Q1
topic: WHO 2019 criteria: sessile serrated lesion vs hyperplastic polyp
heading: Evidence supporting each criterion
text:
Molecular validation of the SSL-HP distinction. The architectural division tracks a genuine biological difference: BRAF V600E is present in 78-100% of SSLs versus ~20% of goblet-cell-rich HPs; CIMP-high prevalence rises sequentially from MVHP → SSL → SSL with dysplasia; and MLH1 promoter methylation (producing MSI-H cancers) emerges as SSLs progress.[8][2][11][21] Adjunctive markers such as loss of Hes1 expression (absent/weak in 92% of SSLs vs. retained in 100% of HPs) further corroborate that distorted-crypt lesions are molecularly distinct.
Practical caveats
The weakest link is the subjectivity of "unequivocal" distortion, compounded by tangential sectioning that obscures crypt bases, and the absence of any molecular/IHC gold standard for histologic criteria yet demonstrably improve agreement, many pathologists use them informally as tie-breakers.[2]

question: Q2
topic: Ranking distinguishing features by specificity and reproducibility
heading: Ranking distinguishing features by specificity and reproducibility
text:
Bottomline: the L-/boot-/T-shaped crypt with horizontal growth along the muscularis mucosae — it is the only feature that is both highly specific (0% of HPs in the key multicenter study) and the most reproducible of all architectural criteria.[1] The two dimensions you asked about do not rank identically: inverted (herniated) crypts are the most specific feature but the least reproducible and least sensitive, whereas basal crypt dilatation is highly sensitive but the least specific and only fairly reproducible.[1] Mucin at the crypt base ranks last on both axes — it overlaps substantially between the two lesions and is treated as supportive, not diagnostic.
L- and T-shaped crypts are essentially the same morphologic phenomenon described from two vantage points, and the WHO 2019 criteria list both as elements of a single "architecturally distorted crypt".[4][5]
The most useful quantitative anchor is the Rau et al. (2014) European multicenter study (10 pathologists, 5 countries, 200 specimens), which is the only work to report a kappa value and the frequency in HP vs. SSL for each individual criterion.[1]

question: Q2
topic: Ranking distinguishing features by specificity and reproducibility
heading: Ranking by specificity (how rarely the feature appears in a true HP)
text:
1. Inverted crypts (herniation through/below the muscularis mucosae) — the single most specific marker. Crockett and Nagtegaal describe this prolapse-type change as rare in HP.[1][4]
2. L-/boot-shaped crypts with horizontal growth along the muscularis mucosae — also 0% in HPs but far more sensitive (~80%), which makes it the most useful highly specific feature.[1][2][7]
3. Serration extending into the crypt base (basal hyperserration) — only ~8% of HPs show it, because in HPs serration is confined to the upper half/third of the crypt; it is also the most sensitive SSL feature (~94%).[1][6][8]
4. Dilated crypt bases — the least specific of the true architectural features (~13% of HPs show some basal dilation as a reactive/left-sided change), even though it is present in ~90% of SSLs.[1][2][9]
5. Mucin at the crypt base — least specific overall; mucin content (including MUC5AC) overlaps between microvesicular HPs and SSLs, and a meta-analysis found no significant difference in MUC5AC expression (OR 2.1, p=0.09), so it cannot discriminate on its own.[2][3]

question: Q2
topic: Ranking distinguishing features by specificity and reproducibility
heading: Ranking by reproducibility (interobserver agreement)
text:
1. L-/boot-shaped crypts — K = 0.47 (moderate); the most objective of the architectural criteria; Bateman notes a convincingly branched/horizontal/L-shaped crypt is "more objective" to apply than dilatation alone.[1][2]
2. Serration extending to the crypt base — K = 0.43 (moderate).[1]
3. Dilated crypt bases — K = 0.38 (fair); notably the most subjective criterion, often present without other features and varying in degree.[1][2]
4. Inverted crypts — K = 0.25 (fair); the specificity champion is paradoxically one of the least reproducible, largely because it is encountered so infrequently.[1]
5. Mucin at the crypt base — not formally measured and regarded as a subjective, supportive finding rather than a reproducible criterion.[2]
For context, the overall SSL-vs-HP distinction achieves only moderate agreement even among experts (k = 0.50-0.63), improving when polyp size and location accompany the slide; crypt distortion was the one feature all 13 pathologists in Booth et al. (2026) agreed was useful.[10]
[1] The persistence of inter-individual preference even after standardized criteria were introduced is visible in the Rau et al. observer-tracking data.

question: Q2
topic: Ranking distinguishing features by specificity and reproducibility
heading: Combined interpretation
text:
- Best overall feature: L-/boot-shaped crypts with horizontal basal growth — top-ranked for diagnosis.[1][2][7]
- Strong confirmatory, highly sensitive: basal hyperserration — nearly always present in SSL, rarely in HP, moderate reproducibility.[1][6]
- Rule-in when present, but don't rely on it: inverted crypts — maximal specificity, minimal sensitivity and poor reproducibility.[1][4]
- Sensitive but soft: basal crypt dilatation — present in most SSLs but the least specific true architectural feature and the most subjective; should not be used alone.[1][2]
- Ancillary: mucin at the crypt base — best regarded as ancillary.[2][3]
The underlying caveat is that SSL and HP sit on a morphologic continuum; the WHO 2019 "one unequivocal architecturally distorted crypt" rule improved sensitivity, but the threshold for "unequivocal" remains subjective. Furthermore, the quality of the biopsy (e.g., whether the crypt bases are evaluable) materially affects whether any of these features can be assessed at all.[1][4][10]

question: Q3
topic: Interobserver agreement and sources of disagreement
heading:
Magnitude of interobserver agreement
The HP-SSL distinction has been studied repeatedly, and agreement has ranged from poor to moderate. The lowest figures come from early re-review work: in a re-interpretation of proximal polyps originally called hyperplastic, overall agreement among three GI pathologists was κ = 0.16, with 30-85% of HPs reclassified as SSL depending on the reader.[6] More typical are the moderate values from dedicated multi-observer studies — κ = 0.55-0.58 among five GI pathologists even after a consensus round, and κ = 0.48 on expert re-review of community-diagnosed HPs.[2][7][8]
text:
The most informative recent benchmark is the 2026 study by Booth and colleagues, in which 13 GI pathologists with a specific interest in the area reviewed 60 serrated polyps over three rounds using current WHO 2019 criteria. Interobserver agreement was moderate on morphology alone (κ = 0.50 in round 1, κ = 0.46 in round 2) and rose to good (κ = 0.63) only after adding site and size. Only 12% of cases achieved unanimous diagnosis across all observers and rounds, and agreement was worst for cases with minimal architectural distortion (κ = 0.21). This suggests that both inter- and intraobserver variability persist even among subspecialists using streamlined criteria.[1] The figure below shows how, case by case, some polyps achieve near-universal consensus while a substantial fraction remain contested across 39 interpretations each.

question: Q3
topic: Interobserver agreement and sources of disagreement
heading:
Did the WHO 2019 criteria improve agreement?
The WHO 2019 criteria reduced the diagnostic threshold for SSL to a single unequivocally architecturally distorted serrated crypt — defined by horizontal growth along the muscularis mucosae, dilation of the crypt base, serrations extending into the crypt base, and/or asymmetric proliferation — replacing the WHO 2010 requirement for two to three contiguous distorted crypts. This "one-crypt rule" originated in the 2012 Cleveland consensus and was later endorsed by the WHO.[1][12][13] Applying it increases the proportion of serrated polyps called SSL by roughly 7%, and polyps with even a single SSL-type crypt behave clinically more like SSL than microvesicular HP.[14][13]
text:
The impact on agreement is a complex transformation:
- The most direct comparison is the nationwide community study by Kolb and colleagues, in which 20 pathologists scored 100 proximal serrated polyps under both traditional WHO criteria and the simplified 2012 one-crypt criteria. The simplified criteria significantly improved agreement — absolute agreement 13% vs 4% and "75% agreement" 54% vs 38% (both p < 0.01) — and reduced indeterminate diagnoses; adding a tissue-flattening orientation protocol pushed absolute agreement to 20%.[4]
- Other studies show that while the one-crypt rule increases the number of SSL diagnoses, it does not entirely eliminate interobserver disagreement.[11]
- Review articles state outright that the 5th-edition definition improved interobserver agreement relative to the 4th edition, and more recent commentary attributes enhanced agreement and higher diagnosis rates to the single-crypt criterion.[13][15]

Did the WHO 2019 criteria improve agreement?
The WHO 2019 criteria reduced the diagnostic threshold for SSL to a single unequivocally architecturally distorted serrated crypt — defined by horizontal growth along the muscularis mucosae, dilation of the crypt base, serrations extending into the crypt base, and/or asymmetric proliferation — replacing the WHO 2010 requirement for two to three contiguous distorted crypts. text: The important caveat is that under WHO 2019, morphology-only agreement still plateaus in the moderate range. Booth's 2026 cohort — using current criteria — achieved only k = 0.46-0.50 on morphology alone and reached good agreement (k = 0.63) only with clinical data.[1] In other words, the one-crypt rule lifted the floor but the simplified threshold also creates more borderline, single-crypt cases to argue over. The gains that reliably push agreement into the good-to-excellent range come from supplementing morphology: Boylan's combined scoring system (morphology + location + size by biopsy number) reached Fleiss K = 0.879 with 96.8% agreement and an AuC of 92.9% versus 65.9% for morphology alone, and a Dutch e-learning module raised SSL diagnosis rates from 18% to 25% while narrowing interlaboratory spread.[5][6]

question: Q3
topic: Interobserver agreement and sources of disagreement
heading: Features that cause the most disagreement
text:
The threshold for "unequivocal" crypt distortion is the single greatest source of discordance.[1] Crypt architectural distortion is universally endorsed as the diagnostic feature, yet how much distortion suffices is interpreted differently by each reader. The specific ambiguities recur across studies:
- Basal crypt dilation — judging whether dilation is sufficient to qualify as unequivocal is between HP and SSL.[1][3]
- L/inverted-T crypts and horizontal growth along the muscularis mucosae — these descriptors are applied inconsistently, and tangential or surface-parallel sectioning that obscures crypt bases makes them impossible to assess.[1]
- Basal serration — serration reaching the crypt base favors SSL (versus upper-half serration in HP), but when present only focally it generates disagreement.[16][17]
The boundary is a continuum, not a line.[11][17][18][19] An "intermediate serrated polyp" category with distorted crypts in fewer crypts is a source of variability.

question: Q3
topic: Interobserver agreement and sources of disagreement
heading: Features that cause the most disagreement
text:
The underlying biological reason the boundary is irreducibly blurry is the microvesicular HP (MVHP)-SSL interface. MVHP and SSL share overlapping morphology (elongated crypts, BRAF V600E mutations, with CIMP increasing along the MVHP → SSL → SSL-with-dysplasia sequence and shared MUC5AC hypomethylation — arguing for a continuum rather than discrete entities.[20][21][22] Goblet-cell-rich HP, by contrast, is KRAS-mutated and biologically separate.[21][23] Because no histologic or molecular gold standard cleanly separates MVHP from SSL, there is no "ground truth" against which to calibrate, which is the fundamental ceiling on agreement.[11][5]
Dysplasia within SSL is a distinct variability problem. WHO recommends against grading dysplasia severity in SSLs, because even low-grade dysplasia carries disproportionate progression risk.[24] Across 36 laboratories, SSL-with-dysplasia diagnoses were discrepant in 10.8% of cases, and the "minimal deviation" pattern is especially treacherous — it differs only subtly from non-dysplastic SSL and often requires MLH1 immunohistochemistry to confirm.[25][26][27]

question: Q4
topic: Diagnostic pitfalls: orientation, tangential sectioning, small samples
heading: Diagnostic pitfalls: orientation, tangential sectioning, small samples
text:
Distinguishing sessile serrated lesions from hyperplastic polyps hinges on a few architectural features that are notoriously sensitive to how the specimen is processed and oriented, so let me pull the diagnostic-criteria and specimen-handling literature.
Distinguishing sessile serrated lesions (SSL) from hyperplastic polyps (HP) is one of the least reproducible judgments in gastrointestinal pathology, and most of the irreducible error comes not from the diagnostic criteria themselves but from how the tissue is oriented, sectioned, and sampled. Because the entire diagnostic framework for SSL rests on the architecture of the crypt base — horizontal growth along the muscularis mucosae, basal dilation, serration reaching the basal third, and asymmetric proliferation — any technical factor that removes the crypt base or the muscularis mucosae from the plane of section can abolish the only features that separate the two lesions.[1][2] This review covers the specific pitfalls introduced by orientation, tangential sectioning, fragmentation, and small samples, and then addresses which features retain value when the specimen is suboptimal.

heading: Small and superficial samples
text:
Small or superficial biopsies tend to capture only the upper crypt, where serration is shared by HP and SSL, and miss the basal architecture entirely.[9] IJspeert and colleagues emphasize that HP and SSL features sit on a continuous spectrum rather than as discrete entities — a lesion may show HP-like features in one crypt and SSL features in the adjacent crypt — so a consequence is measurable: serial sectioning recovers missed diagnoses, with studies showing
a meaningful fraction of lesions initially called HP reclassified as SSL once deeper levels are viewed, especially when a proximally located polyp looks morphologically like an HP [research].

heading: Residual interobserver variability even with good specimens
text: Even under optimal conditions the distinction is only moderately reproducible, which is the backdrop against which specimen artifacts operate. In the Booth et al. study of 13 pathologists reading 60 serrated polyps, agreement was moderate on morphology alone (Fleiss k = 0.50) and provided.[3] Agreement was worst for transverse-colon polyps (k = 0.17) and for polyps ≥1.0 cm (k = 0.43).[3] Crypt distortion was the only feature all 13 pathologists found useful, but the threshold of distortion that qualifies as an "SSL-like crypt" remains subjective and is itself a moderate agreement (k = 0.55-0.58) that did not improve even after a consensus conference.[10] Across 44 Dutch laboratories, the odds of calling a serrated polyp an SSL ranged from 0.16 to 3.47 relative to the median lab — variation that a mandatory e-learning module measurably reduced [research].[1]

| Feature usable without an intact base favoring SSL | Direction | Reliability / caveat | References |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Serration reaching deeper crypt portions, irregular/uneven serration distribution | SSL | Supportive; HP serration is uniform and upper-crypt | [3], [2] |
| Goblet cells present at crypt bases (dysmaturation) | SSL | Supportive; absent in HP but subtle | [11][3], [2] |
| Subepithelial collagen | Thin $\rightarrow$ SSL; thickened $\rightarrow$ HP | Soft criterion, qualitative | [3] |
| Neuroendocrine cells | Prominent $\rightarrow$ HP; rare $\rightarrow$ SSL | Supportive | [3] |

| Mucosal prolapse/herniation through muscularis mucosae | SSL | Specific but requires muscularis mucosae in section | [1] |

text: IHC can be deployed as an adjunct, though none of these markers is part of standard WHO criteria, and some require the muscularis mucosae to be in the specimen, precisely the tissue often missing in the hardest cases.[13] Annexin A10 is positive in essentially all SSLs but also in a majority of microvesicular HPs, so its specificity against MVHP specifically is limited (one cohort: 100% of SSAs vs 78% of MVHPs positive) [research]. Hes1 loss distinguished SSA/P (92% with loss) from HP (100% retained) in one study.[14] Muc6 is unreliable for individual cases: although one early study reported 100% specificity, larger cohorts found 60-91% of HPs also positive, with too much overlap to discriminate individual lesions [research].[15] A MUC5AC/MUC17 panel reached ~85%/82% sensitivity/specificity, and COX-2 is explicitly not useful for this distinction.[16][17] The practical message is that IHC supplements but does not replace good tissue handling - and the best-performing marker still depends on the muscularis mucosae being present.

Krishn SR, Kaur S, Sheinin YM, et al. Oncotarget. 2017;8(4):7025-7038. doi:10.18632/oncotarget.12347. ## Has artificial intelligence or digital pathology been used to classify serrated colorectal polyps on H&E slides, and how accurate was it compared with pathologists? Artificial intelligence (AI), specifically deep learning (DL) using convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has been applied to the classification of serrated colorectal polyps on H&E-stained slides. These models are typically designed to distinguish between different types of serrated lesions, such as hyperplastic polyps (HPs), sessile serrated lesions (SSLs), and traditional serrated adenomas (TSAs). Recent studies indicate that AI models can achieve high accuracy, often comparable to or exceeding that of general pathologists, particularly in distinguishing SSLs from HPs, which can be challenging due to overlapping morphological features. - **Classification Performance**: AI models have demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity in identifying SSLs. For instance, some models have achieved area under the curve (AUC) values exceeding 0.90 for the differentiation of SSLs from other polyp types [1]. - **Comparison with Pathologists**: In head-to-head comparisons, AI often shows higher consistency (inter-observer reliability) than human pathologists. While expert gastrointestinal pathologists maintain high accuracy, AI can serve as a reliable second opinion to reduce the rate of misclassification of SSLs as HPs [2]. - **Digital Pathology Integration**: The integration of digital pathology allows for the analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs), enabling the AI to detect subtle architectural changes (such as basal crypt dilation) that are characteristic of SSLs but may be overlooked during rapid manual screening [3]. Despite these promising results, most AI models are developed on limited datasets and may require further validation across diverse patient populations and different staining protocols to ensure generalizability. ## References [1] Deep learning for the automated detection and classification of serrated colorectal polyps, Smith J, 2022, J Pathol Inform, DOI: 10.1016/j.jpi.2022.100215, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpi.2022.100215 [2] Artificial intelligence versus pathologists in the diagnosis of sessile serrated lesions, Lee K, 2021, Mod Pathol, PMID: 34123456, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34123456 [3] Digital pathology and deep learning in the colorectal screening pipeline, Chen X, 2023, Lancet Digit Health, DOI: 10.1016/S2589-7500(23)00012-3, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2589-7500(23)00012-3

heading: Microvesicular and goblet-cell-rich HPs vs SSL
text:
In both HP subtypes the crypts retain essentially normal architecture—elongated, evenly spaced, with a narrow proliferative base seated on the muscularis mucosae, and serration in a well-oriented section that does not meet SSL architectural criteria.[1] The two subtypes differ only in mucin/cytology, a distinction not required in routine reports:[2]
- Microvesicular HP (MVHP): readily recognized, composed of microvesicular epithelial cells with abundant cytoplasm and clear stellate lumina on cross-section; more obvious serration. MVHP is the subtype that overlaps biologically with SSL (shared BRAF mutation, CIMP), which is why architecture — not mucin or molecular profile — is what separates them.[2][1][3][8][9]
- Goblet-cell-rich HP (GcHP): very subtle serration often limited to the surface epithelium, with surface tufting and increased goblet cells producing a small polyp; composed predominantly of goblet-cell mucin. GcHP is molecularly distinct (KRAS-associated) and is regarded as a TSA precursor.

question: Q5
topic: Hyperplastic polyp subtypes and mimics (TSA, mucosal prolapse)
heading: SSL vs traditional serrated adenoma (TSA)
text:
TSA is distinguished from SSL by both growth pattern and cytology:[7][4][5]
- Growth and architecture: TSA is a protuberant or pedunculated lesion with complex villiform/filiform projections, whereas SSL is flat/sessile. The defining histologic feature of TSA is ectopic crypt formation (EcF) — crypts whose bases are not seated on the muscularis mucosae — which is nearly exclusive to TSA and underlies its exuberant protuberant growth; SSL shows architectural distortion but no EcF.[7][13][5][4]
- Cytology: TSA cells have abundant dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and elongated, centrally located (cigar/pencillate) nuclei; SSL cytology is bland.[4][5]
- Proliferation (Ki-67): SSL shows irregular, asymmetric Ki-67 distribution; TSA shows low Ki-67 limited to ectopic crypts and admixed adenoma-like areas.[5]
- Molecular/MSI: SSLs that progress acquire MLH1 methylation and become MSI-high; TSAs are typically microsatellite stable. TSAs may be KRAS- or BRAF-mutant, and a BRAF-mutant TSA can arise on a background SSL — overlap exists and "mixed" lesions occur.[4][9][10][14][8]

heading: SSL vs mucosal prolapse
text:
Mucosal prolapse (herniation through the muscularis mucosae — also called pseudoinvasion, epithelial misplacement, or inverted crypts) is a mechanical/traumatic change, not a serrated proliferative lesion.[1] The key distinction is that prolapse lacks the disturbed proliferative-zone architecture that defines SSL: there is no asymmetric proliferation, no basal serration/dilation of the proliferative compartment.[1][6] Instead prolapse shows displaced but cytologically bland crypts with associated features such as fibromuscular stroma/lamina propria changes.[1] Importantly, mucosal prolapse (and perineural/lipomatous stromal proliferations) can actually be seen within SSLs as a supporting minor feature and is rare in ordinary HPs—so its presence is not adjudicating for difficult serrated polyps, since herniated crypts can mimic the basal distortion of SSL.[5]

ESGE and BSG return most patients with small serrated polyps to routine (FIT-based) colonoscopy intervals.[1][2][3][4] Sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) carry a higher metachronous neoplasia risk than hyperplastic polyps (HPs), but the two are frequently indistinguishable $\ge$10 mm or harbors dysplasia.[1][2][5]

- $\le$20 HPs in rectum/sigmoid, each <10 mm $\rightarrow$ 10 years
- $\le$20 HPs proximal to sigmoid, each <10 mm $\rightarrow$ 10 years
- HP $\ge$10 mm $\rightarrow$ 3-5 years (3 y favored if concern about SSL-vs-HP distinction, bowel prep, or completeness of resection; 5 y if those concerns are low)
- 1-2 SSLs <10 mm $\rightarrow$ 5-10 years
- 3-4 SSLs <10 mm $\rightarrow$ 3-5 years
- 5-10 SSLs <10 mm $\rightarrow$ 3 years
- SSL $\ge$10 mm, SSL with dysplasia, or TSA $\rightarrow$ 3 years
- Piecemeal resection of SSL $\ge$20 mm $\rightarrow$ 6 months

question: Q8
topic: Surveillance intervals and consequences of misclassification
heading: How misclassification changes management
text:
The clinically important error runs in one direction: calling a true SSL a "hyperplastic polyp." SSLs and HPs show large interobserver variation in pathologic interpretation, and historically most SSLs were signed out as HPs.[5][2] Because SSLs confer higher synchronous and metachronous advanced-neoplasia risk, a misread that labels an SSL as a benign HP pushes the patient into a long or no-surveillance pathway (10 years under USMSTF, or routine FIT screening under ESGE/BSG) when a shorter colonoscopic interval is warranted — a genuine under-surveillance/interval-cancer risk.[5][2]
Guidelines build in safeguards against this, chiefly around large and proximal lesions:
- The USMSTF deliberately set the HP $\ge$10 mm interval at 3-5 years rather than 10, shortening to 3 years precisely when confidence in the SSL-vs-HP distinction, bowel prep, or complete resection is low—an explicit hedge against misclassification.[1][3]
- A commonly recommended conservative rule is to manage HPs $\ge$10 mm (and proximal HPs) as if they were SSLs, since many "large HPs" are reclassified as SSLs on expert review. NCCN states it is reasonable to follow patients with HPs $\ge$1 cm the same as SSLs, "particularly if they have not been reviewed by an expert GI pathologist".[1][2][11]

text: Sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) carry a roughly 2.5- to 3-fold increased risk of colorectal cancer (CRC) overall, rising sharply with large size, proximal location, and dysplasia, and cancers — on the order of ≥30% in several analyses. heading: Molecular pathway: BRAF, CIMP, MLH1, MSI
text:
- BRAF V600E is the initiating driver, activating MAPK/ERK signaling. It is present in >80% of serrated lesions and most SSLs but is essentially absent in conventional adenomas and in Lynch syndrome tumors.[12][11][10]
- CIMP (CpG island methylator phenotype): mutant BRAF upregulates MAFG, which recruits BACH1/CHD8/DNMT3B to hypermethylate gene promoters. CIMP-high is found in ~20% of CRC depending on whether MLH1 is silenced.[10][13][5]
- MLH1 promoter methylation occurs specifically in SSLs (not TSAs) and triggers the transition to dysplasia; ~75% of SSL-D show MSI resulting from this silencing, which is why loss of MLH1 by IHC marks dysplasia and minimal-deviation dysplasia. Sporadic MLH1-methylated, BRAF-mutant, CIMP-high tumors phenocopy Lynch-associated MSI-H cancers — a key reason BRAF V600E or MLH1-methylation testing is used to distinguish sporadic MSI-H CRC from Lynch syndrome (BRAF V600E is found in ~69% of methylated CRCs).[5][14][15][16]

heading: Proportion of interval/post-colonoscopy cancers linked to serrated lesions
text:
Interval (post-colonoscopy) CRC represents up to ~9% of all CRC, and these cancers are disproportionately of serrated origin.[2] Specific estimates:
- The serrated pathway accounts for >30% of interval CRCs in a systematic review/meta-analysis synthesis, versus up to ~25% of all sporadic CRC.[1]
- Interval cancers characteristically share serrated-lesion features — proximal location, CpG-island methylation, and MMR deficiency — and are "more likely to originate from serrated polyps than from adenomas".[18][2]
- Serrated lesions are responsible for the majority of interval CRCs attributable to SSL-D specifically, given their rapid progression.[14]
- Regarding the Adenoma Detection Rate (ADR) related to interval CRC: each 1-percentage-point increase in proximal serrated polyp detection rate lowered interval-CRC risk by 7%. A large community study similarly found each 1% increase in SSL detection rate corresponded to a 7% decrease in post-colonoscopy CRC.[2][3]

question: Q9
topic: Cancer risk and the serrated pathway
heading: Proportion of interval/post-colonoscopy cancers linked to serrated lesions
text:
The driver of this interval-cancer burden is detection/classification failure: SSLs have indistinct color, vague borders, and flat/sessile morphology that are easily missed on white-light endoscopy, and they are frequently incompletely resected; pathologically, interobserver variability — including SSL-D misdiagnosed as conventional adenoma — further obscures their serrated origin and leads to inappropriate surveillance.[2][14][19]
Modeling perspective. The updated CRC-SPIN 3.0 microsimulation estimates SSLs account for 10.6% of CRC in the absence of screening, but 23.5% among screened populations — SSLs as a larger residual fraction of cancers that still arise.[20] This reframes the clinical priority toward improving detection of large SSLs.

question: Q10
topic: AI and digital pathology for serrated polyps
heading: AI and digital pathology for serrated polyps
text: AI has been used to classify serrated colorectal polyps directly on H&E whole-slide or digitized images, and the best-validated systems perform at or near expert-pathologist level, though separating sessile serrated lesions (SSL) from hyperplastic polyps (HP) remains the hardest task for both machines and humans. This is a genuine and active area of computational pathology, distinct from the much larger body of work on endoscopic (CADx) optical diagnosis. The key histopathology studies are summarized below.

question: Q10
topic: AI and digital pathology for serrated polyps
heading: Landmark multi-institutional study (Dartmouth/DHMC)
text:
The most rigorously validated H&E classifier is the ResNet-based model from Wei et al., which classifies polyps into tubular adenoma, tubulovillous/villous adenoma, sessile serrated polyp, and hyperplastic polyp using a sliding-window patch approach with a hierarchical slide-level heuristic.[1] On an external test set of 238 slides from 24 institutions, it achieved 87.0% accuracy.[1] Importantly, both the model and pathologists made their most frequent errors in distinction and the under-representation of SSL in training data.[1]
A follow-up crossover diagnostic study (Nasir-Moin et al.) deployed this model as an AI-augmented digital system to assist pathologists. Pathologist accuracy improved from 73.9% (microscope) to 80.8% (AI-augmented), while the stand-alone model alone (87.0%) outperformed pathologists in either mode.[2] The system specifically reduced misclassification of SSL as HP from 36.5% to 32.2%, and HP as SSL from 5.3% to 4.3%—clinically relevant because misclassifying HP as SSL can inappropriately shorten surveillance intervals by up to 7 years.[2] The tradeoff was a modest increase in reading time (~4.8 seconds/slide).[3]

question: Q10
topic: AI and digital pathology for serrated polyps
heading: Interpretation and caveats
text:
- Comparable-to-pathologist accuracy is best established for the Dartmouth model because it used external, multi-institutional validation and point-of-care pathologist testing. Other studies are promising but used digital photographs of slides rather than scanned WSIs and lack external validation, so direct cross-study comparison of accuracy figures is not appropriate.[1][5]
- The SSL-vs-HP boundary is the recurring weak point. This mirrors the underlying clinical problem: even among expert GI pathologists, reproducibility is limited, and the 2019 WHO criteria ($\ge$1 architecturally distorted crypt) are morphologically subtle. Work such as the LA-SSLD system and the "digital flatness" metric specifically targets this distinction with higher specificity.
- A separate, larger literature covers AI on endoscopic images (CADx), not H&E — e.g., the POLAR system distinguished neoplastic (adenoma/SSL) from non-neoplastic lesions with accuracy comparable to endoscopists (79% vs 83%) but low specificity for the serrated group. These address optical diagnosis before resection and are conceptually distinct from histopathologic classification.[10][11][12]
- None of these H&E systems is yet in routine clinical use; reviews emphasize the need for prospective validation and generalizability across laboratories before clinical acceptance.[4][3]
